# Investigation Report: 2023 3CX DesktopApp Software Supply-Chain Compromise

## Executive Summary

The strongest publicly documented evidence indicates that the 2023 3CX DesktopApp compromise was initiated through a prior compromise of software distributed by Trading Technologies. According to Mandiant, a 3CX employee’s computer had previously acquired a maliciously modified version of the X_TRADER application from the legitimate Trading Technologies website. That initial compromise enabled the threat actor to obtain access to the 3CX environment, move laterally, compromise both Windows and macOS build infrastructure, and ultimately tamper with 3CX’s DesktopApp installers. The compromised installers were then distributed to 3CX customers as apparently legitimate, digitally signed software. ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

This makes the incident a cascading or chained software-supply-chain compromise: an earlier software supply-chain compromise involving Trading Technologies enabled a second software supply-chain compromise involving 3CX. Mandiant stated that this was the first such cascading software-supply-chain compromise it had identified. ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

The public attribution is not expressed uniformly across reporting. Mandiant tracked the activity as **UNC4736**, described it as a suspected North Korean nexus cluster, and assessed with moderate confidence that it was related to financially motivated North Korean AppleJeus activity. Kaspersky attributed the deployment of the Gopuram backdoor to **Lazarus** with medium-to-high confidence. CrowdStrike publicly associated the operation with **Labyrinth Chollima**, while other reporting used names such as Kimsuky, Emerald Sleet, or Velvet Chollima. The most defensible conclusion is that the 3CX operation was publicly associated with a North Korea-linked, financially motivated activity cluster, but that the precise relationship among UNC4736, Lazarus, AppleJeus, Labyrinth Chollima, and other naming schemes remained subject to analytic uncertainty. ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise); [Kaspersky, 2023](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/); [Cybersecurity Dive, 2023](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/supply-chain-attack-3cx-desktop-thousands/646432/))

## Scope and Source Assessment

This report reconstructs the evidence chain using the supplied public reporting. Sources were weighted according to their proximity to the underlying investigation:

| Source | Role in reconstruction | Principal evidentiary value |
|---|---|---|
| Mandiant / Google Cloud | Incident-response and malware investigation | Initial intrusion vector, lateral movement, build-environment compromise, malware chain, cluster assessment |
| Kaspersky Securelist | Independent telemetry and malware analysis | Gopuram deployment, selective targeting, Lazarus assessment, victim profile |
| Singapore Cyber Security Agency | Government advisory | Affected versions, capabilities, recommended response |
| CrowdStrike reporting as reproduced by Cybersecurity Dive | Early detection and operational observations | Signed-binary activity, suspected Labyrinth Chollima attribution, scale indicators |
| WIRED | Investigative reporting and synthesis | Human-readable account of the chained compromise and attribution disagreements |
| Google Threat Analysis Group | Earlier AppleJeus-related campaign reporting | Context for North Korean cryptocurrency targeting and Trading Technologies infrastructure overlap |
| MITRE ATT&CK | Structured threat-intelligence reference | Relationship of AppleJeus and Lazarus Group; associated techniques and aliases |

Mandiant’s account is the most important source for the initiation and propagation questions because it reports findings from an incident response involving 3CX. Kaspersky provides independent corroboration for the selective deployment of Gopuram and the cryptocurrency focus. Government and ATT&CK sources are useful for validating affected versions and historical actor relationships but do not independently establish every step of the 3CX intrusion.

## Reconstruction of the Public Evidence Chain

### 1. The initial compromise occurred through Trading Technologies software

Mandiant identified a tampered installer for **X_TRADER**, a software package provided by Trading Technologies. The installer was named `X_TRADER_r7.17.90p608.exe` and had the MD5 hash `ef4ab22e565684424b4142b1294f1f4d`. Mandiant reported that the installer was still available from the legitimate Trading Technologies website in 2022, despite the X_TRADER platform reportedly having been discontinued in 2020. ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

The malicious X_TRADER installer was digitally signed under the subject “Trading Technologies International, Inc.” It contained a signed `Setup.exe`, which dropped malicious DLLs and a benign executable. The benign executable was used to side-load a malicious DLL. The loading chain used SIGFLIP and DAVESHELL to decrypt and execute the VEILEDSIGNAL modular backdoor. ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

Mandiant’s central finding was that a malware-laced X_TRADER package downloaded from the Trading Technologies website was the initial compromise vector into 3CX’s network. The supplied evidence does not establish how Trading Technologies’ website or X_TRADER installer was originally compromised, nor does it establish the full number of victims of that earlier compromise. Mandiant specifically indicated that it had not been hired by Trading Technologies to investigate the original compromise. ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

WIRED reported the operational consequence of that finding: a 3CX employee’s computer had been compromised after the employee installed the infected X_TRADER application. The infected machine provided the adversary with a foothold from which access could be expanded through the 3CX network. ([WIRED, 2023a](https://www.wired.com/story/3cx-supply-chain-attack-times-two))

There is a contextual qualification. Trading Technologies told WIRED that X_TRADER was a tool for trading professionals and that there was no apparent reason for it to have been installed on a 3CX machine. Trading Technologies also stated that 3CX was not its customer and that the compromise did not affect its current software. These statements do not invalidate Mandiant’s technical finding, but they leave some operational details about how the software arrived on the employee’s computer unresolved. ([WIRED, 2023a](https://www.wired.com/story/3cx-supply-chain-attack-times-two))

### 2. The attacker used the initial foothold to compromise 3CX’s internal environment

Mandiant reconstructed an intrusion in which the threat actor harvested credentials and moved laterally within 3CX. The attacker used a compiled version of the open-source Fast Reverse Proxy project for lateral movement. Mandiant identified a file named `MsMpEng.exe`, with MD5 `19dbffec4e359a198daf4ffca1ab9165`, dropped in `C:\Windows\System32`. ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

The available evidence indicates that the attacker’s objective was not limited to compromising one employee workstation. The actor progressed from the infected endpoint into the 3CX corporate environment, harvested credentials, moved laterally, and eventually reached the company’s software build systems. This transition from endpoint compromise to build-environment compromise was the critical escalation that enabled the later supply-chain attack.

### 3. Both Windows and macOS build environments were compromised

Mandiant reported that the attacker compromised both the Windows and macOS build environments used by 3CX.

On the Windows build environment, the attacker deployed:

- **TAXHAUL**, a launcher;
- **COLDCAT**, a downloader; and
- persistence through DLL search-order hijacking involving the IKEEXT service, with execution under LocalSystem privileges.

On the macOS build server, the attacker deployed **POOLRAT**, using Launch Daemons for persistence. Mandiant clarified that a sample previously described by other reporting as a new malware family, SIMPLESEA, was instead determined to be POOLRAT. ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

The macOS finding is significant because it shows that the compromise reached the development and build infrastructure across more than one operating-system platform. However, this should not be confused with certainty that the customer-facing malicious payload executed equally across Windows and macOS endpoints. Early reporting stated that activity had been observed on Windows and macOS, while other researchers had not independently confirmed macOS activity at that stage. ([Cybersecurity Dive, 2023](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/supply-chain-attack-3cx-desktop-thousands/646432/))

### 4. The 3CX DesktopApp build and distribution process was poisoned

The compromised build environment allowed the attacker to insert malicious code into legitimate 3CX DesktopApp software. Mandiant reported that the affected software included **3CX DesktopApp version 18.12.416 and earlier**. The malicious code ran a downloader named **SUDDENICON**, which retrieved additional command-and-control server information from encrypted icon files hosted in a GitHub repository. A later component, **ICONICSTEALER**, collected browser information. ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

Kaspersky similarly reported that the malicious MSI installers contained an infected DLL. That DLL decrypted shellcode stored in the overlay of `d3dcompiler_47.dll`, extracted command-and-control URLs from icons in a GitHub repository, and downloaded an information-stealing payload. The infostealer collected system information and browser history. ([Kaspersky, 2023](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/))

The attack was particularly effective because the malicious application was distributed as a legitimate 3CX product and was signed by 3CX. Early reporting described “unexpected malicious activity from a legitimate signed binary,” including beaconing, deployment of second-stage payloads, and—in a small number of cases—hands-on-keyboard activity. ([Cybersecurity Dive, 2023](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/supply-chain-attack-3cx-desktop-thousands/646432/))

The Singapore Cyber Security Agency identified the following affected versions:

| Platform | Affected versions reported by CSA |
|---|---|
| Windows Electron application | 18.12.407 and 18.12.416 |
| macOS Electron application | 18.11.1213, 18.12.402, 18.12.407, and 18.12.416 |

The advisory described capabilities including system-information harvesting and theft of data and stored credentials from Chrome, Edge, Brave, and Firefox profiles. ([Cyber Security Agency of Singapore, 2023](https://www.csa.gov.sg/alerts-and-advisories/alerts/al-2023-040/))

### 5. The compromised software created a broad exposure but a narrow second-stage targeting operation

3CX stated that its technology was used by more than 600,000 corporate customers and had more than 12 million active daily users. Huntress reported more than 242,000 publicly exposed 3CX phone-management systems based on Shodan data and said it had sent 2,595 incident reports involving a maliciously hashed `3CXDesktopApp.exe` signed by 3CX. These figures describe potential exposure and observed indicators; they do not establish that all potentially exposed systems were compromised or that all affected systems received the same follow-on payload. ([Cybersecurity Dive, 2023](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/supply-chain-attack-3cx-desktop-thousands/646432/))

Kaspersky observed that the attackers did not deploy the most capable backdoor to every infected system. It identified fewer than ten machines, at least within its telemetry, where the **Gopuram** backdoor was deployed. Kaspersky described this as “surgical precision” and found a specific interest in cryptocurrency companies. It did not identify evidence of actual cryptocurrency theft in the cases it observed. ([Kaspersky, 2023](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/))

Gopuram provided broader post-compromise functionality than the initial browser-information stealer. Kaspersky described capabilities for file-system interaction, process creation, registry manipulation, service management, timestomping, process injection, and execution of additional in-memory modules. ([Kaspersky, 2023](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/))

## Threat-Activity Attribution

### Mandiant’s UNC4736 assessment

Mandiant tracked the activity as **UNC4736**, a suspected North Korean nexus cluster. It assessed with moderate confidence that UNC4736 was related to financially motivated North Korean **AppleJeus** activity. Mandiant based this assessment on overlapping malware, infrastructure, loading techniques, and a sustained focus on cryptocurrency and fintech-related services. ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

Mandiant identified several technical similarities between the X_TRADER and 3CX compromises:

- use of the same RC4 key, `3jB(2bsG#@c7`;
- use of SIGFLIP;
- reliance on DAVESHELL;
- use of the hard-coded cookie variable `__tutma`; and
- use of AES-256-GCM encryption.

Mandiant considered this shared loading and encryption infrastructure important evidence connecting the earlier Trading Technologies compromise with the later 3CX compromise. ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

### Kaspersky’s Lazarus assessment

Kaspersky attributed the Gopuram deployment to **Lazarus** with medium-to-high confidence. Its reasoning included the prior observation of Gopuram coexisting with AppleJeus on a Southeast Asian cryptocurrency-company victim, overlap between infrastructure used by Gopuram and AppleJeus, and connections to domains previously attributed to Lazarus. Kaspersky also observed the Gopuram activity in fewer than ten infected machines and found that the targeted victims included cryptocurrency companies. ([Kaspersky, 2023](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/))

MITRE ATT&CK identifies AppleJeus as malware used by Lazarus Group and describes AppleJeus as a family of downloaders embedded in trojanized cryptocurrency applications. The entry associates AppleJeus with Windows and macOS activity and with targeting across financial, technology, telecommunications, government, and other sectors. ([MITRE ATT&CK, n.d.-a](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0584/))

MITRE’s Lazarus Group entry describes Lazarus as a North Korean state-sponsored group and lists associated names including Labyrinth Chollima, HIDDEN COBRA, ZINC, NICKEL ACADEMY, and Diamond Sleet. It also cautions that North Korean cyber units may share personnel, infrastructure, malware, and tradecraft, making high-confidence separation of individual operators difficult. ([MITRE ATT&CK, n.d.-b](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0032/))

### Alternative public naming

Early reporting based on CrowdStrike research associated the operation with **Labyrinth Chollima**, a North Korea-linked threat actor active since at least 2009. ([Cybersecurity Dive, 2023](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/supply-chain-attack-3cx-desktop-thousands/646432/))

A WIRED article discussing Mandiant’s findings used several names—“Kimsuky,” “Emerald Sleet,” and “Velvet Chollima”—for the hacker group. Those labels should be treated as a reporting inconsistency rather than as independently established proof that all names refer to a single operational unit in this incident. ([WIRED, 2023a](https://www.wired.com/story/3cx-supply-chain-attack-times-two))

Google TAG’s earlier reporting provides relevant context but not direct proof of responsibility for the 3CX compromise. TAG documented North Korean activity targeting cryptocurrency and fintech users through Operation AppleJeus, including compromise of the Trading Technologies website in February 2022. Mandiant used that prior Trading Technologies activity as corroborating context for its UNC4736 assessment. ([Google Threat Analysis Group, 2022](https://blog.google/threat-analysis-group/countering-threats-north-korea/); [Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

## Findings

### Finding 1: How was the 3CX compromise initiated?

The best-supported answer is that a 3CX employee’s machine was compromised through a maliciously modified X_TRADER installer downloaded from the legitimate Trading Technologies website. The evidence does not establish how the original Trading Technologies compromise occurred or the complete population of victims of that earlier attack.

### Finding 2: How did the compromise propagate?

The attacker used the X_TRADER-derived foothold to harvest credentials and move laterally through the 3CX environment. The attacker then compromised Windows and macOS build servers, established persistence, and modified the software-development and build environment.

### Finding 3: How did the compromise reach customers?

The attacker inserted malicious functionality into 3CX DesktopApp installers. Those installers were distributed as signed, legitimate-looking software. The initial payload downloaded further infrastructure and an information-stealing component; selected victims received Gopuram, a more capable modular backdoor.

### Finding 4: What was the public attribution?

The most precise incident-specific designation is **UNC4736**, a suspected North Korean nexus cluster. Mandiant assessed with moderate confidence that it was related to financially motivated North Korean AppleJeus activity. Kaspersky assessed the Gopuram deployment as likely Lazarus activity with medium-to-high confidence. These assessments are mutually directionally consistent but do not prove that all public labels—Lazarus, Labyrinth Chollima, AppleJeus, UNC4736, Kimsuky, Emerald Sleet, and Velvet Chollima—represent one identical operational entity.

## Overall Assessment

The public evidence supports a high-confidence reconstruction of the **technical chain**:

**Compromised Trading Technologies X_TRADER installer → infected 3CX employee workstation → credential harvesting and lateral movement → compromise of 3CX build environments → trojanized signed 3CX DesktopApp releases → broad customer exposure → selective deployment of information stealers and Gopuram.**

The evidence supports a strong but carefully qualified attribution to a North Korea-linked, financially motivated cyber activity cluster. My assessment is that **UNC4736 is the most appropriate incident-specific analytic label**, while **Lazarus/AppleJeus** is the strongest public contextual association. Labyrinth Chollima and other names should be retained as alternative vendor nomenclature rather than treated as independently confirmed identities. The evidence demonstrates intent consistent with cryptocurrency theft, but the supplied sources do not establish that cryptocurrency was actually stolen from the observed victims.
